entries.localizedLabel: Visit an amusement park, fair, or circus venue
entries.localizedDescription: Enter an amusement park, fair, or circus venue as a guest for leisure. A ride, a purchase, or watching a particular show may be tracked as a distinct activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Visit a zoo, aquarium, botanical garden, or flower show
entries.localizedDescription: Visit a zoo, aquarium, botanical or safari park, or flower show to view organized collections or displays. Searching for a species in the wild is a different activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Attend an amateur match or competition
entries.localizedDescription: Attend a local or amateur match or competition as a spectator and watch participants at the venue. This entry emphasizes a grassroots or local event, not viewing on a screen.

entries.localizedLabel: Watch a motorsport race in person
entries.localizedDescription: Watch a motorsport race as a spectator at the track or viewing area. Spectating is not driving the vehicle or watching an online broadcast.

entries.localizedLabel: Watch a sports competition in person
entries.localizedDescription: Be at the venue as a spectator and watch a live sports competition. Watching a home or online broadcast and taking part as an athlete are different activities.

Use and move miniature figures to act out a scene in a chosen game or an imagined scenario, assigning them roles. If you use a battle-system ruleset, it is a wargame; without one, it is freeform play.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a collectible or trading card game
entries.localizedDescription: Play a collectible card game using a personal deck assembled before the match from cards acquired or traded outside it. This is deck construction and play, not a card market or collecting as a separate activity.

Play a deck-builder that starts with a small shared or starter deck and lets players acquire or add cards during the game. This differs from a TCG, where a personal collectible deck is usually built before play.
Play dominoes by matching suitable ends or building a chain according to the chosen variant’s rules. Collecting domino tiles is a separate activity.
Play Go by placing stones on grid intersections and surrounding territory or an opponent’s stones. Playing a game and independently studying Go problems are distinct activities.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a social deduction or Mafia game
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in a hidden-team game by discussing suspicions and voting or acting to identify secret roles. Discussion-based deduction distinguishes it from games where every role is public.
Play a game in which cards are the main components: draw, play or discard cards, or collect combinations according to the rules. Specify a narrower subgenre separately.
Play a Living Card Game (LCG): build a deck from fixed products and play an encounter or scenario. Random collectible booster packs are not the basis for expansion in this model.
Play tabletop mahjong by drawing and discarding tiles to form a valid winning hand. This is not Mahjong Solitaire, which matches pairs.
Play a skirmish scenario with a small squad or individual fighters, emphasizing individual movement, cover, and small-scale conflict. This is a wargame subgenre, not every game that uses miniatures.
Play backgammon by rolling dice, moving checkers along points, and bearing them off according to the rules of the short or long version. Random rolls affect the available moves.

Play a tabletop game by taking turns making moves or decisions with components under the rules of one game. This is a broad category; specify the title, genre, and player count separately when useful.

Take part as a player in a tabletop RPG by describing a character’s actions and making decisions in a shared imagined situation with a game master or rules. Scenario preparation and the GM role are separate aspects.
Play a short social game for a group, with simple, quickly explained prompts, votes, or team rounds. “Party” describes the audience format, not a single game mechanic.
Play a chess game by taking turns moving pieces on a checkered board to checkmate the king. Analyzing a game, learning moves, and watching a match are different activities.
Play a trick-taking game in which participants play one card each into a trick, and rank or trump suit determines who takes it. Scoring depends on the game’s rules.

Play a miniature wargame by moving unit figures across a battlefield or terrain and resolving combat and objectives under scenario rules. The miniatures are game pieces; assembling or painting them is separate.
Play out a military-history scenario with models or tokens, using rules for the forces, era, and course of battle. The historical period or battle is the game’s theme, not a separate sport.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a role-playing game by post
entries.localizedDescription: Play a character and advance a role-playing story through messages or posts, with pauses between turns. The asynchronous format differs from a real-time game session.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in a live-action role-playing game
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in a live-action role-playing game by embodying a character and acting or interacting with others in a physical space under agreed rules and a scenario. Cosplay without role-play is not by itself LARP.
localizedAliases: Take part in a live-action game

entries.localizedLabel: Run a tabletop RPG as the game master
entries.localizedDescription: Run a tabletop role-playing session as the game master by describing the setting, running NPCs and the scenario, and adjudicating the group’s actions under the rules. This is the GM role, not that of a player character.
localizedAliases: Run a tabletop RPG as GM

entries.localizedDescription: Act out a story or freely interact with toys or figures, assigning roles and actions. Assembling a model or construction set may be a related creative phase.

entries.localizedLabel: Play with LEGO or a construction set
entries.localizedDescription: Build, rebuild, or use LEGO or another construction set in free play. An engineering build designed to perform a specified function may be a separate activity.
Play a game whose success depends on inventing, forming, or guessing words, such as word chains or associations, in turns or against a timer. Reading a word puzzle is a different format.
Lay out and move cards for one player according to set rules, aiming to build sequences or foundation piles. It remains a solo game even when played digitally.
Solve puzzles printed in a book by reading the clues and writing down or checking an answer. The book is the medium; crossword and logic puzzles are possible puzzle types.

entries.localizedLabel: Solve a puzzle in an app
entries.localizedDescription: Interact with a puzzle in an app and check solutions on a screen or by touch. The phone is the platform; the puzzle type defines the logical goal.
Fill intersecting squares with words using written clues and letters already revealed. Solving word clues is the defining mechanism of a crossword.
Derive a solution from a puzzle’s conditions or constraints by eliminating impossible options. Specify a particular logic-puzzle type separately if useful.
Solve a puzzle by reading short clues placed inside the grid and entering words in the indicated direction. Unlike a standard crossword, its clues are embedded in the grid.
Fill a grid with digits or symbols without repeating them in the rows, columns, or specified blocks. This is a logical-constraint puzzle, not arithmetic calculation.
Answer a logic problem from text or a diagram by drawing conclusions from its conditions. This is solving a posed problem, not a competitive game.

entries.localizedLabel: Solve a Rubik’s Cube or speedcube
entries.localizedDescription: Turn the faces of a twisty puzzle, such as a Rubik’s Cube, to restore the target color arrangement. Speedcubing is a distinct timed-solving format, not every relaxed solve.
Match pieces by shape and image to form one flat picture, usually without turns or competition. A three-dimensional mechanical puzzle works differently.
Build a three-dimensional or mechanical construction puzzle from interlocking pieces by shape or instructions until it forms a stable model. This is not assembling a flat jigsaw picture.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a co-op or party video game
entries.localizedDescription: Play a cooperative video game or a video game designed for a group with others. Specify cooperative mode or party format separately when useful.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a fitness or dance game
entries.localizedDescription: Play a game where dance moves or exercises are recognized as input and affect score or progress. Physical exercise may also be a separate meaning for the same time interval.
Play a digital game whose progress requires solving embedded spatial or logic puzzles. Track the platform or title separately; do not conflate it with a paper puzzle.
Read and choose branches in an interactive narrative, making decisions that change the story’s course or ending. This is narrative interactivity, not watching a video or reading an unchanged novel.
Control an interactive game on a computer using a chosen input method. PC identifies the platform; genre and online, co-op, or PvP mode are separate dimensions.
Play on a home or handheld game console with a controller or other standard input. Genre, solo or online mode, and service are separate details.
Play a digital game on a phone or tablet using touch or buttons. Mobile describes the device, not a genre or a requirement that sessions be short.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a digital version of a tabletop game
entries.localizedDescription: Play a round of a digital implementation of a particular tabletop game, making moves on screen or online. The tabletop game’s mechanics remain, but physical components are absent.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a cloud or streamed game
entries.localizedDescription: Play through a cloud gaming stream: commands come from the user’s device while the remote computer’s image and processing are delivered over the network. This describes access or delivery, not a game genre.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a solo or online video game
entries.localizedDescription: Play a solo or online video game, alone, together with others, or against other players.

entries.localizedLabel: Play an online RPG or MMORPG
entries.localizedDescription: Play an online RPG or MMORPG by controlling a character, completing quests, fighting, or exploring a persistent shared virtual world with other participants. Social play does not necessarily mean PvP.

Control a virtual system, machine, or process modeled with its own constraints, such as flight, transport, or farming. “Simulator” describes resemblance to a system, not a training or certification goal.

entries.localizedLabel: Play a VR or XR game
entries.localizedDescription: Play an interactive VR or XR environment by controlling a character or objects through a headset and controller or gestures. VR or XR describes presence and interface, not a game genre by itself.

entries.localizedLabel: Compete in an esports match or tournament
entries.localizedDescription: Play as a participant in an organized esports match, league, or tournament under its rules and compete for a result. Watching a tournament, a practice session, and organizing a team are separate activities.
Spin or start a slot machine and place a wager to receive a random combination or payout. A digital game with no real money and an arcade game machine may be separate cases.
Play a casino game under its probability-based rules, with or without a money wager or prize, such as a table game. Specify the game mechanics (roulette, blackjack, etc.) and stake separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in a lottery or prize draw
entries.localizedDescription: Buy a ticket, register, or choose a number in a lottery and wait for a random prize draw. Without a money stake, it may be a free promotional draw rather than gambling.
localizedAliases: Take part in a prize draw

entries.localizedDescription: Take part over the internet in gambling or a wager involving money or value. This is a channel for different forms of gambling, not a distinct game mechanic; clarify whether real stakes are involved.

entries.localizedLabel: Play poker for money or in a tournament
entries.localizedDescription: Play a poker game or tournament with money stakes or a prize pool, making decisions about hidden cards, bets, and community cards. Poker as a no-stakes hobby or strategy study is a separate case.

entries.localizedLabel: Bet on sports or horse racing
entries.localizedDescription: Choose an outcome in a sports event or horse race and place a wager, then check the result or settlement. The sporting event itself and watching a race are not betting.
Browse forum threads and replies to follow the discussion. Reading a particular post or writing a reply is separate participation.

entries.localizedLabel: Scroll through short videos or a social feed
entries.localizedDescription: Scroll through a personalized feed of short videos or posts, moving between items without selecting one specific piece. Stopping to watch an individual video may be a separate activity.
Move between pages or sites out of curiosity without one preselected article. Purposefully reading a page or searching for a practical answer is different.
Choose a future movie or video, time, or viewing companions. This is planning, not watching the content itself.
Search and compare titles in a service catalog to choose something to watch or listen to later. Playback of the selected work has not started.
Listen to a narrated book, in full or in excerpts. Audio is not the same as reading with your eyes, though it may happen alongside another activity.
Listen to a dramatized audio work whose story is conveyed through voices, effects, and sound. This differs from reading a play or watching an adaptation.

entries.localizedLabel: Listen to ambient sound or a recording
entries.localizedDescription: Listen to a soundscape or ambient composition as audio content. Playback device and relaxation goal are session attributes.

entries.localizedLabel: Listen to music, an album, or a playlist
entries.localizedDescription: Listen to a music recording, album, or playlist. A live performance, playing an instrument, and dancing to it may be concurrent but distinct tags.
Listen to an audio podcast episode. Hosting or producing the episode and watching a video version are different activities.
Listen to live radio broadcasting or a recording of it. The station, receiver, or app is the source or means.

entries.localizedLabel: Listen to a talk or lecture for leisure
entries.localizedDescription: Listen to an oral presentation or lecture in free time. Whether it is a study or work obligation depends on context and is not required.
localizedAliases: Listen to a lecture for leisure

entries.localizedLabel: Listen to a live audio stream or room
entries.localizedDescription: Join a live audio room or voice stream as a listener. Speaking through a microphone and hosting the broadcast may be separate or simultaneous activities.
localizedAliases: Listen to a live audio stream

entries.localizedDescription: Read a chosen text while at a library. “Library reading” describes the place or context; reading and visiting the library can be tracked separately or at the same time.
Read a selected post, page, or article on a blog or website. Browsing a feed and moving between different items may be a separate practice; the source does not imply a reading purpose.
Read an extended analytical or technical report or document, focusing on its text. Work or study obligation may change the context, not the activity.
Read a book on an e-reader or tablet screen. The device and digital medium describe access format, not the text’s genre.
Read fan-authored fiction based on someone else’s universe or characters. The work is the object; reading is the activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Read a forum or social media post
entries.localizedDescription: Read a selected message, post, or discussion on a forum or social network. Writing a reply and moving between posts are separate activities; the user’s reason for reading is not inferred.

entries.localizedLabel: Read a book, novel, or poetry
entries.localizedDescription: Read an extended, continuous text such as a book, novel, or poetry collection. The precise genre and medium describe content or format, not a separate physical activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Read a comic, manga, or graphic novel
entries.localizedDescription: Read a sequential story combining images and words, moving through panels or pages. This differs from watching an adaptation or looking at standalone images.
Read written news reports or articles about current events. A video segment or radio broadcast is a different channel.
Read a periodic or one-time email newsletter or bulletin. Processing work email is a different context, though it uses the same channel.
Read one complete piece or article in print or digital form. Viewing an entire page without selecting a text is browsing.
Read an issue of a periodical containing a selection of articles or news. Newspapers and magazines differ in editorial format, not in the basic act of reading.
Watch an animated film or episode, including anime. Technique or genre describes the work, not a live performance.
Watch a film or other cinematic work of any length on a screen at home, in a theater, or while traveling. Viewing location and cinema event are context, not limits on length.

entries.localizedLabel: Watch gameplay or a Let’s Play video
entries.localizedDescription: Watch a recorded video-game playthrough or commentary without controlling the character yourself. Playing interactively and watching a game stream are different modes of participation.
Watch a live or recorded video-game competition as a spectator. Playing the same game is not the same as watching a match.

Watch one or more selected online videos, including short videos. Scrolling through a feed between videos may be tagged as a separate interaction mode; no viewing purpose or lack of purpose is implied.
Watch one or more episodes of a series that continues across installments. The title and platform are the content and source.
Watch a broadcast of a sports match or competition on a screen. Attending in person as a spectator and taking part in the sport are other activities.
Watch a live stream or broadcast in real time, possibly with chat. Hosting the stream or playing or performing on air is a creator activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Watch a TV program or reality show
entries.localizedDescription: Watch a television program, reality show, or other formatted episode. Unlike a film, this is a broadcast-format program or series.
Watch the video version of a podcast conversation or episode. An audio-only episode is listened to, and producing an episode is a separate activity.

entries.localizedLabel: Watch a recorded lecture or video blog
entries.localizedDescription: Watch a previously recorded lecture or video blog. Watching is the activity; learning purpose, creator intent, and subject matter are separate details.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in an adventure or multisport race
entries.localizedDescription: Compete in a multidiscipline adventure race with a route or checkpoints and whatever navigation the organizer requires. The course may be marked or may require participants to choose their own route. Race stages, disciplines (often running or trekking, cycling, and paddling), transitions, and team format vary. The whole event and its stages may appear as overlapping time views and should not be added together as separate time.
Jump from a height while attached to an elastic cord that stretches and rebounds. A parachute is not the primary means of descent.
Jump from a fixed high structure or cliff with a parachute system that opens after exit. This is not a jump from an aircraft or a bungee jump.
Fly a rigid delta wing in a suspended harness and steer by shifting body weight. A rigid frame and weight-shift control distinguish it from paragliding.

entries.localizedLabel: Fly in a hot-air balloon or other balloon
entries.localizedDescription: Fly in the basket of a balloon while the pilot controls altitude and direction with the wind in mind. The envelope may be lifted by hot air or gas, so this category is not limited to hot-air balloons. A passenger sightseeing flight and piloting are different roles.
Launch beneath a flexible canopy wing and fly by steering its lines or shifting body position. A paraglider folds and does not have the rigid delta frame of a hang glider.

entries.localizedLabel: Skydive or make a parachute jump
entries.localizedDescription: Make a sport or recreational jump from a suitable aircraft, such as a plane or helicopter, using a chosen deployment method: freefall with manual opening, automatic or static-line opening, or a tandem system. Do not imply that every jump includes freefall; distinguish this from a BASE jump from a fixed object.

Ride along a tensioned cable on a zipline or progress through a series of ropes-course obstacles. A zipline is one cable crossing; a ropes course is a sequence of platforms or obstacles; a park is the venue.
Practice ballet technique, such as positions, plié, relevé, and barre or center combinations, or perform choreography. A lesson or rehearsal differs from a stage performance.
Perform partnered ballroom dances in standard or Latin technique during training, a social dance, or a competition. The exact dance program and event are optional details.
Learn or perform choreography inspired by Indian cinema or popular stage performance, combining gestures and steps. Do not assume one universal Indian traditional style.
Perform breaking by combining toprock, downrock or footwork, freezes, and power moves in a round or practice session. A battle or stage event and individual practice are different contexts.
Practice jazz dance through isolations, rhythmic steps or jumps, and choreography in a chosen stage style. Jazz dance is movement, not listening to jazz music.
Dance hip-hop choreography or freestyle using groove and selected street-dance styles or moves. Choreography, battles, and open practice are possible formats.

entries.localizedLabel: Create choreography or rehearse a dance combination
entries.localizedDescription: This category preserves both creating choreography (inventing or staging a sequence of movements and choosing music and space) and rehearsing a completed combination (repeating and refining an already defined sequence). These are related but distinct creative and performance phases.

entries.localizedLabel: Dance Latin or social styles such as salsa, bachata, tango, and swing
entries.localizedDescription: Dance or learn a selected social style, such as salsa, bachata, tango, swing, West Coast Swing, or lindy hop. Each has its own steps and musical tradition; the list does not describe one standard dance.
localizedAliases: Social dance styles: salsa, bachata, tango, swing, West Coast Swing, and lindy hop

entries.localizedDescription: Perform a folk or traditional dance alone or in a group. Specify the region and tradition separately when useful.
Dance as a pair, coordinating steps, leading, and following to music. Specify a style such as tango, salsa, or ballroom separately; this is not one single genre.

Perform dance or acrobatic elements on a vertical pole or an aerial apparatus such as silks, hoop, or trapeze. Pole and aerial forms use different equipment and techniques and may be tracked separately.
Repeat acting or movement, blocking, and cues for a stage production. Preparing a show differs from the public performance itself and from attending as a spectator.
Dance with a partner or group in a relaxed social setting to music, following an agreed style. This is taking part in dance, not a lesson or rehearsal or watching a performance.
Practice contemporary dance through set or improvised choreography and work with weight, floor, impulse, and space. A specific school or performance is not required.

entries.localizedLabel: Do a dance workout or cardio session
entries.localizedDescription: Repeat continuous dance combinations for physical exertion. Distinguish a fitness or cardio class from a social dance event or stage rehearsal.
Create rhythmic patterns with steps in shoes fitted with metal taps, striking the floor to make sound. Dancing and a separate music recording are different activities.
Practice aikido through partner drills on entering, balance, throws, and joint-control techniques. The chosen school or practice determines technical emphasis and contact level.
Train or take part in a boxing match, using permitted punches with protective gloves. Kicks and wrestling are outside the basic boxing format.
Wrestle by throwing or controlling an opponent with holds above the waist. Holds and attacks involving the legs are restricted by the rules, distinguishing it from freestyle wrestling.
Practice freestyle wrestling by attacking or defending with holds and takedowns, using arms and legs for attacks or defense under the style’s rules.
Train in BJJ by working on grips, control, and submissions, primarily on the ground. Grappling is a broader family of styles and rules, not a synonym for BJJ.
Practice judo with throws, holds, and permitted joint locks or chokes depending on the competition category. Its format and rules differ from BJJ.
Fence with a chosen weapon—foil, épée, or sabre—and make touches or strikes under its rules. The weapon type provides further detail.
Practice capoeira in a roda, combining musical rhythm, evasions, strikes, acrobatic movements, and play with a partner. It is not simply dancing to music.
Practice hand and foot strikes, defenses, and forms (kata) in a chosen karate school. Sparring, kata, and basic technique are different forms of the same practice.
Fence with a bamboo shinai while wearing armor and practice stances or striking lines under kendo rules. This is not foil, sabre, or épée fencing.
Train punches and kicks in a kickboxing style or ruleset. Whether knees, clinching, and particular target areas are allowed depends on the organization.
Have a controlled practice bout with a partner under chosen rules and contact level. Technical drills and a competitive fight are different formats.
Practice a chosen Chinese martial-arts style or sport wushu: forms, stances, strikes or weapons, or competition routines. The terms cover different schools and are not exact synonyms.
Train or compete in mixed martial arts, combining striking, wrestling, and ground control under MMA rules. It combines disciplines and is not a synonym for grappling.
Train in Thai boxing with punches, kicks, elbows, knees, and clinch work under Muay Thai rules.
Train in sambo with throws, holds, and submission techniques under the chosen sport or combat rules. Specify the particular sambo format separately.
Practice taekwondo, where sport formats place substantial emphasis on kicks as well as stances, blocks, and forms. Specify kyorugi or poomsae rules when relevant.
Repeat sports techniques or moves in exercises without requiring a full bout. Specify the discipline and techniques separately; tag sparring only when it is actually happening.
Perform a workout combination using a ballet barre or an equivalent support, mixing small strength and mobility movements. This does not have to be a classical ballet class.
Intentionally practice exercises for breathing rhythm or control. If used as part of yoga, meditation, or singing, an overlapping tag may be retained.
Practice basic gymnastics exercises for coordination, flexibility, balance, and strength. No particular competitive discipline is implied.
Do a chosen practice of poses, breathing, and/or focused movement within yoga. No particular style or goal is assumed.
Perform a series of small, controlled contractions and held poses for muscular endurance or control. No brand or instructor is required.

entries.localizedLabel: Practice mobility or joint range of motion
entries.localizedDescription: Perform controlled movement through joint ranges and work on active mobility. This differs from holding a static stretch.
Perform a sequence of controlled Pilates exercises for strength, core control, and mobility. Mat or equipment and the style are details.
Hold or repeat positions and movements to increase the range of motion of muscles or joints. A warm-up or rehabilitation program may be the context but is not implied.
Practice a chosen form of taijiquan through sequences, transitions, or paired and applied exercises with body control. Pace may be slow or fast depending on the school or format.

entries.localizedLabel: Do a dance workout or dance aerobics
entries.localizedDescription: Repeat choreographed movements for a fitness workout. A dance class or cardio format and social dancing are different possible contexts.

entries.localizedLabel: Practice qigong or kung fu exercises
entries.localizedDescription: Perform a sequence of calm movements, postures, breathing, and attention known as qigong. Its purpose may be health, spiritual practice, or study. Kung fu form or technique drills are a separate choice, even when both occur in one session.

entries.localizedLabel: Cool down or do a recovery workout
entries.localizedDescription: This combined category covers either (1) a cooldown after exertion, gradually lowering intensity with light movement or breathing, or (2) a separate recovery workout with gentle mobility, breathing, or low-intensity work at another time. Rest without exercise remains a different activity.
Perform continuous or interval aerobic choreography to music. No specific dance style is implied.

entries.localizedLabel: Do water aerobics or aquatic fitness
entries.localizedDescription: Perform an organized set of aerobic movements in water. Equipment, depth, and intensity are parameters; swimming laps is a separate mode.
Run on a motorized or manual treadmill. The treadmill is the equipment or location, not a separate running discipline.

entries.localizedLabel: Jog or run at an easy pace
entries.localizedDescription: Run at a conversational or comfortable pace for ordinary aerobic exercise. The type does not specify distance or surface.

entries.localizedLabel: Do a running workout on a track
entries.localizedDescription: Run a workout at a stadium or on a track. Specify the running format, such as intervals, recovery, or tempo, separately.
Do a group or solo general-conditioning workout combining strength and aerobic exercises. Equipment and team format may vary.
Do a prolonged continuous or nearly continuous run. “Long” is relative to the training plan; it is not a distinct speed.
Play a game in which body movement is part of the controls or task and creates physical exertion. Record the game title and input device separately if useful.
Perform rowing strokes on a stationary rowing ergometer. This is machine training, not rowing a boat.
Alternate short high-intensity intervals with recovery periods. HIIT describes workout structure, not a particular exercise.
Repeat running segments at a set intensity, alternating them with recovery intervals. The workout plan defines the pattern.
Jump rope alone or in sets for coordination or cardio. Tricks and interval formats are possible session variations.
Perform several exercises in sequence at stations or blocks, with short transitions. The exercise mix defines the workout.
Combine several types of cardio in one workout. The exercises remain identifiable components, but the combined activity can also be used as a single entry.
Swim repeated pool lengths as a workout session. Specify stroke, intervals, and pool separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Do fitness walking, Nordic walking, or racewalking
entries.localizedDescription: Walk for exercise, including Nordic walking with poles. Specify the technique if useful: regular fitness walking, Nordic walking, or racewalking.
Perform choreographed aerobic steps on a platform to music. Platform height and combination difficulty are workout parameters.

entries.localizedLabel: Work out on an elliptical trainer
entries.localizedDescription: Do a cyclical cardio workout on an elliptical trainer, moving arms and legs. Resistance and program are session parameters.

entries.localizedLabel: Work out on a stepper or stair machine
entries.localizedDescription: Repeat a climbing step on a stepper or stair machine for cardio training. The machine type specifies the equipment.
localizedAliases: Work out on a stair machine

entries.localizedDescription: Walk at an intentional pace as a distinct physical workout. A walk for leisure or transportation depends on context; specify speed and route separately.
Ride a bicycle outdoors as a dedicated workout, with sustained or interval effort. The equipment and route are context; a trip for transportation may have a different tracking meaning.

entries.localizedLabel: Do stationary cycling, spinning, or indoor cycling
entries.localizedDescription: Pedal a stationary bicycle or indoor cycle for a solo workout or an instructor-led workout set to music. The bike and studio format are details.
Ride a handcycle with a chosen manual or assistive configuration. The activity is handcycle riding; “adaptive” describes access or equipment, not a diagnosis or a required competition class.

Ride a scooter by pushing off the ground with one foot and steering with the handlebar. Trick scootering, a casual ride, and a route to a destination are distinct modes; an electric scooter is not implied.
Ride a longboard while dancing on the moving board or making a downhill run. Specify the riding style separately if useful.
Skate on roller skates with wheels arranged in a line (inline) or in pairs (quad). Speed, slalom, dance, figure elements, and route are different skating modes.
Play a contact team sport on roller skates around an oval track, scoring as the designated player passes opposing players. This is not simply recreational skating.
Glide on skis with roller wheels over a hard surface, using poles and a ski stride to train outside snow season. This is not roller skating.

entries.localizedLabel: Skateboard in street, park, or vert
entries.localizedDescription: Ride a skateboard and push or perform tricks at a chosen street spot, skatepark ramps, or vert ramp. Surface or style and competition format can be specified separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Do a wheelchair push workout or racing-chair event
entries.localizedDescription: Train physical endurance and technique by propelling a wheelchair with the arms, and/or take part in a sports race in a racing chair. Training and competition may be separate activities; an ordinary everyday trip is a different context.
Advance an oval ball through carries, passes, and offensive or defensive plays under American football rules. This is not soccer or rugby.
Play Australian rules football by handpassing or kicking an oval ball and advancing it toward the goals under Australian football rules.
Dribble or pass the ball and shoot it into a basket. Player count and rule variant are session parameters.
Play three-on-three basketball at one hoop. This is a distinct, shorter basketball format, not a general tag for any small court.
Play baseball by alternating pitching or hitting the ball with advancing around bases under the chosen version’s rules. Baseball and softball are related but distinct games.
Play a chosen sport involving a flying disc. Specify the sport, such as ultimate, disc golf, or freestyle, when precise tracking matters.

entries.localizedLabel: Play dodgeball or a local dodgeball variant
entries.localizedDescription: Play dodgeball or a local variant by dodging and throwing balls under that game’s rules. The term “vyshibaly” may refer to locally specific rules.
Play flag football by stopping an opponent’s advance by removing a flag instead of making a forceful tackle. Specify the rules format separately.
Play indoor floorball with lightweight plastic sticks and a light ball. This is not ice hockey or field hockey.
Pass and dribble the ball with the feet and try to score goals in association football. This differs from American or Australian football and from watching a match.
Play futsal or a chosen small-sided football format on a reduced-size pitch. “Mini-football” can mean different local rules, so specify the rules when needed.

Play court handball by passing or dribbling the ball with the hands and throwing at goal. Standard indoor play has seven players per side on the court and differs from beach handball, a four-player sand game with set-based or specialized scoring.
Play Gaelic football by combining foot kicks, handpasses or hand strikes, and scoring into or over the goal under Gaelic rules.
Play field hockey on grass or an artificial surface, moving a ball with a stick under field hockey rules. The surface and rules distinguish it from ice hockey, floorball, and inline hockey.
Play ice hockey on ice, skating and controlling a puck with a stick.
Play kickball by kicking a rolled ball and advancing around bases. Rules may vary by league.
Pass the ball and shoot it into a high basket under korfball’s team and zone rules.
Play cricket by batting and defending the wickets, then taking fielding and bowling roles. Match formats can vary considerably.
Catch, pass, and shoot a ball with a netted stick. Format and contact level depend on the version of the rules.
Control figures on rotating rods to play a match of table football or foosball. This is not playing regular football.
Pass the ball among players and shoot at the rings under netball’s movement and zone rules.
Play handball on sand in teams of four players on court, advancing and throwing the ball into the goal. The format uses sets and scores spectacular goals differently from an indoor court match.
Play volleyball on a sand court. The standard beach format has two teams of two, with no indoor rotation and a different surface; four-on-four and recreational rules are also possible.
Play full-sided rugby union with 15 players per team: advance the oval ball by running and backward passes, make tackles, and score under union rules.
Play the seven-a-side version of rugby union. The reduced team size and match structure are part of this chosen format.
Play rugby league under its possession and play-the-ball system. Do not automatically combine it with rugby union 15s or sevens.
Play sepak takraw by sending a woven ball over a net using the feet, head, and body, without using the hands.

Play a baseball-related game with batting and base running under softball’s own rules. In international fast-pitch, the ball is pitched underhand; the official softball ball and field or distance dimensions differ from baseball. Slow-pitch and local variants retain their own rules, so softball is not a synonym for baseball.
Play ultimate by advancing a disc through passes and catches toward a scoring zone, without moving while holding the disc.
Play water polo in the water by passing and throwing a ball into the goal. Swimming is part of the game but is not a separate lap-swimming workout.

Play volleyball on a hard court in the standard indoor format, receiving, passing, and attacking the ball over the net. Teams usually have six players on court and rotate. This is not beach volleyball’s two-on-two format on sand.
Operate a four-wheel ATV or quad on permitted dirt terrain or trails. A recreational ride, trail riding, and racing are different goals; the quad is the vehicle.

entries.localizedLabel: Do autocross or a track session
entries.localizedDescription: This combined entry covers three possible meanings: (1) FIA autocross, a competition on a closed natural dirt or unpaved circuit, often with several cars at once; (2) U.S. SCCA autocross or Solo, driving a short cone course one car at a time in a parking lot or airfield for the best time; and (3) a track race or time trial on a paved circuit. Specify the region and track type: “autocross” is ambiguous across these formats.
Ride a horse around three barrels in the prescribed cloverleaf pattern against the clock. This is a distinct Western riding event.
Ride a horse to catch a calf and throw or secure a lasso under calf-roping rules. The rider’s role and rope work distinguish it from ordinary riding or horse racing.
Drive a small go-kart on a closed paved or indoor track for practice or a race. This is motor circuit sport, not sim racing.

entries.localizedLabel: Do show jumping, dressage, or eventing
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in show jumping, dressage, or equestrian eventing: clear obstacles, perform riding movements, or combine dressage, cross-country, and show jumping.
Ride as part of a team and use a mallet to direct a ball into the opposing goal. Working with the horse and team play distinguish polo from ordinary horseback riding.

entries.localizedLabel: Ride a motorcycle on a closed track
entries.localizedDescription: Ride a motorcycle on a closed circuit or motorcycle track for practice or a session. Motorcycle type and track-day or race format are details; off-road motocross and enduro use different courses.
Ride a motorcycle off-road in motocross or enduro format. Specify the discipline and route type separately if useful.
Participate in a rodeo event, with the specific event—such as riding a bull or horse, or roping—chosen separately. “Rodeo” may refer to a whole program of contests, not one fixed sport.
Compete on a motorized snowmobile on a snow or ice course, controlling acceleration and line. An ordinary recreational snowmobile ride is not necessarily a race.

entries.localizedLabel: Race stock cars or drag race
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in stock-car racing on a circuit or oval, or in straight-line drag racing. Specify the race format separately if useful.
Ride a horse and guide its direction or gait during a lesson or recreational ride. Specify a particular equestrian discipline, such as dressage or show jumping, separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Practice aerial arts or pole sport
entries.localizedDescription: Practice aerial acrobatics on a chosen apparatus, such as silks, hoop, or trapeze, or pole sport. Specify apparatus and goal, such as dance, tricks, or strength training, separately if useful.
Perform gymnastic or partner acrobatic elements—balances, inversions, rolls, and lifts—in an individual or group format. Specify a particular sport separately.
Run a distance while clearing hurdles set in sequence along the lane. The approach and clearance rhythm distinguish this from a flat sprint.

entries.localizedLabel: Do trampoline gymnastics or recreational jumping
entries.localizedDescription: Perform controlled bounces and aerial elements on a trampoline. Competitive trampoline, recreational bouncing, and trampoline-park jumping are different session modes.

entries.localizedLabel: Run, race walk, or relay on a track
entries.localizedDescription: Run, race walk, or take part in a relay on an athletics track.
Perform a team routine with chants or dance, jumps, pyramids or stunts, and tumbling for support or competition. This is more than dance and does not necessarily occur at a sports match.
Take part in track-and-field throws: throw a discus, hammer, or javelin, or put the shot.

entries.localizedLabel: Compete in a track-and-field combined event
entries.localizedDescription: Score points across a series of different running, jumping, and throwing events. The whole meet and each attempt may be related but should not be counted twice.

entries.localizedLabel: Do high jump, long jump, or pole vault
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in the high jump, long jump, or pole vault. Specify the event separately.
Practice artistic gymnastics on apparatus or rhythmic gymnastics with apparatus and choreographed routines.

Run a short distance with maximum acceleration, starting from a position or blocks and aiming to cross the finish as quickly as possible. This is track sprinting, not swimming; swimming has its own “swimming sprint” type.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in an adventure race
entries.localizedDescription: Compete in a multidiscipline adventure race by following a route and checkpoints and combining running or trekking, cycling, water, or other stages according to the organizer’s format.

entries.localizedLabel: Mountaineer or climb on natural terrain
entries.localizedDescription: Climb natural rock or follow a mountaineering route in mountain terrain. A route may include hiking, scrambling or easy climbing, snow or ice, and navigation. Technical roped climbing is one option, not required for every ascent.
Run on a stationary treadmill. The movement is still running; the machine’s motor, speed, and incline are equipment or session settings, not a race type.
Run on a cross-country course, field, or varied terrain. Unlike road running, the route usually follows natural ground, though “cross-country” and “trail running” overlap regionally.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in obstacle course racing
entries.localizedDescription: Run a course while successively clearing organized physical obstacles. Navigation and switching sports are not required, so OCR is not the same as an adventure race.
Find designated checkpoints in terrain by choosing a route with a map or compass under competition rules. Running is common, but orienteering is not limited to running.
Walk at a comfortable or brisk pace for physical activity or well-being. This need not be a structured workout and does not define a walk for transportation.
Move through urban or natural obstacles by running, jumping, climbing over, and landing. Freerunning more often includes showy tricks; specify the style without treating the terms as exact synonyms.

entries.localizedLabel: Hike as a training or sports session
entries.localizedDescription: Walk a long-distance or hilly route as physical training. A hike without a training focus can remain outdoor recreation; particular route sections or an overnight stay are related phases.
Walk briskly with purposeful arm movement. No required speed or technique is specified; distinguish this from competitive racewalking.

In a team rogaining race, plan a route among checkpoints within a time limit and score points for the checkpoints visited. Unlike ordinary orienteering, it is a long-duration team format with freedom over checkpoint order and value.

entries.localizedLabel: Ruck or walk with a loaded pack
entries.localizedDescription: Walk with a loaded backpack for training or challenge. Carrying a load is a defining difference from an ordinary walk; route and pack weight are session parameters.

Run an ultrarunning or ultramarathon distance, defined in the cited World Athletics description as longer than a standard 42.195 km marathon. The organizer sets the event’s distance and format; training for an ultra remains a running workout unless the user chooses to track an event.
Run on natural trails or varied terrain, adjusting your stride to the surface and elevation. Trail running does not require a competition.

entries.localizedLabel: Trek or climb to a summit
entries.localizedDescription: Complete a long-distance or mountain walking route (trekking), or climb toward a specified summit or goal. Route travel and reaching a summit may overlap, but one does not necessarily mean the other.

Play blind football under a chosen format, usually with an audible ball and agreed communication. Paralympic materials also use the name Football 5-a-side. Outside that context, other five-a-side games may follow different rules and are not automatically blind football.
Run with a chosen companion or guide runner, using an agreed way to communicate and navigate. The guide is a participation format, not a separate movement or an assumption about diagnosis.
Play boccia by rolling or throwing leather balls toward the target jack. Under class rules, delivery may be by hand, foot, ramp, or an assistant.
Roll a ball with bells toward the opposing goal and defend your own line on the court. Hearing the ball and participants’ silence are part of the game.

entries.localizedLabel: Handcycle or take part in para cycling
entries.localizedDescription: This combined label preserves both handcycling (pedaling a bicycle by hand in a handcycle or recumbent hand position) and the broader para-cycling category: adapted cycling or racing on a handcycle, tricycle, tandem with a pilot, or a conventional bicycle in the relevant class. Do not reduce para cycling to handcycles or infer a diagnosis from the equipment.
Shoot a bow at a target in a chosen para-archery format, using a position or support suited to the participant and discipline rules. Do not infer a class from the equipment.
Play badminton in a para class under the chosen rules, moving while standing or using a wheelchair according to the category. The activity is badminton, not a separate mobility method.
Paddle a chosen canoe or kayak in a para format to propel the boat. Class and adaptations to the boat or seating are optional or set by the rules.

entries.localizedLabel: Take part in para equestrian sport
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in a para equestrian competition or training session by guiding a horse in a chosen discipline, usually para dressage. Class and adaptations describe the participation format.
Perform a competitive bench press under para powerlifting rules. This para discipline does not imply squats or deadlifts as in powerlifting training.
Row in an adapted boat or crew discipline using a suitable body position and equipment. The event, class, and boat are event attributes.
Swim or compete in a race under adapted para-swimming classes and rules. Start or assistance method, stroke, and distance are specified by the event, not inferred as a diagnosis.
Complete the swim, cycling, and running or wheelchair legs in a para-triathlon event or workout. Class, equipment, and stages are event parameters.
Race in a specialized sports wheelchair by pushing the wheels on a track or road course. Distance and class describe the event, not mobility in general.
Play volleyball while seated on the floor, moving the body and arms, blocking, and sending the ball over the net under sitting-volleyball rules.

entries.localizedLabel: Play sled hockey or para ice hockey
entries.localizedDescription: Play ice hockey on a sled, using two specialized sticks both to propel and steer and to shoot the puck. Sled hockey is a distinct format, not a synonym for conventional ice hockey.
Play badminton in a wheelchair under the relevant court and classification format, serving and returning the shuttle with a racket. Do not infer a particular class from the activity name.
Play basketball in a sports wheelchair, maneuvering the chair and dribbling, passing, or shooting the ball into the basket. Chair-movement rules are part of the game format.

Play wheelchair curling by delivering a stone from a wheelchair toward the house, using a chosen release or assistance method, and strategizing around the stones. Stone delivery and whether sweeping is allowed depend on the format.
Fence with a chosen weapon while seated or secured in a special frame, attacking the valid target and defending under fencing rules. Weapons are foil, épée, or sabre.
Play wheelchair rugby in a specialized chair, advancing or passing the ball toward a scoring zone under this distinct game’s contact rules. This is not conventional rugby.
Rally a tennis ball with a racket while moving in a sports wheelchair. Wheelchair tennis includes an allowed adapted bounce and is not identical to conventional tennis.

entries.localizedLabel: Do adapted yoga or mobility practice
entries.localizedDescription: Practice yoga or joint mobility using chosen supports, positions, or ranges of motion. These are two base practices; adaptation describes access and need not be a separate activity type.
Alpine ski using a sit-ski and chosen assistance or lift access. The access equipment and slope format can be specified separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Row or paddle with an adaptation
entries.localizedDescription: Row (propel a boat with oars) or paddle (use a bladed paddle) with a chosen adaptation to position, equipment, or assistance. These are different actions but share a user-facing shortcut.
Perform strength exercises while seated with chosen resistance or equipment. “Seated” describes position or access, not a muscle group or diagnosis.
Ride a snowboard on snow using a chosen adaptation or position. The possibility of adaptation does not mean every participant uses a sit-ski or another specific setup.
Train by propelling a manual wheelchair independently: cover a distance, do intervals, or take part in a race.

entries.localizedLabel: Do handcycling in an adaptive format
entries.localizedDescription: Ride a handcycle. “Adaptive format” describes the equipment or access, not a separate movement activity or an inference about medical status.
Hit a shuttlecock over a net with a racket, aiming to make it land on the opponent’s court. The shuttle’s flight distinguishes the game from racket sports played with a ball.
Rally a lightweight ball across a table net with small rackets. The short rallies and table distinguish table tennis from court tennis.
Play padel on an enclosed court with a racket and ball, using the walls or enclosure as part of rallies under padel rules. Do not confuse it with platform tennis or POP Tennis.
Play pickleball with a solid paddle and a hollow perforated ball on a court over a low net. Its equipment and rules distinguish it from padel and platform tennis.

entries.localizedLabel: Play platform tennis or paddle tennis
entries.localizedDescription: Play platform tennis on a small raised court with an enclosure, using a solid paddle and a special ball. Another use of the name “paddle tennis” may refer to POP Tennis.
Play beach tennis on a sand court over a net, hitting the ball with a racket before it lands. The surface and rules distinguish it from regular tennis.
Hit a rubber ball with a racket against the walls and play out a point in an enclosed court under racquetball rules. Do not use this as a name for squash.
Play historic real or court tennis on an asymmetric enclosed court with walls, galleries, and special markings. This is not ordinary tennis or platform tennis.
In an enclosed court, hit a ball with a racket so it rebounds from the front wall. Side and back walls are part of play under squash rules.
Rally a ball with a racket over a net and within the court boundaries. Singles or doubles, surface, class, and practice are optional details.
Perform a prescribed or self-developed set of physiotherapy movements at home. The location does not turn the exercise into household work; prescription and goal are separate details.
Perform a set of graded therapeutic physical exercises under a chosen or prescribed program. Treatment or rehabilitation is context.
Perform controlled tasks for stability, weight transfer, and balance. These may be part of training or rehabilitation.
Perform exercises during recovery after an injury. Specify the movement separately; a recovery phase does not imply a particular diagnosis.
Do strength training to develop muscle size or shape. Hypertrophy is the goal; bodybuilding is a sport or aesthetic practice.

entries.localizedLabel: Do circuit or station-based strength training
entries.localizedDescription: Move through strength-work stations in a circuit with short rests. Exercises may use weights or bodyweight.
Perform a workout combining changing strength, gymnastics, and metabolic movements in the style of a chosen functional program. Branded CrossFit and general functional fitness are not exact synonyms.
Perform strength movements selected for coordination and transfer of effort to everyday or sports activities. A coach’s label alone does not specify a diagnosis or goal.
Train or compete in the squat, bench press, and deadlift under powerlifting rules. Do not conflate it with Olympic weightlifting.

entries.localizedLabel: Lift with a barbell, dumbbells, or kettlebells
entries.localizedDescription: Perform strength sets with weights such as a barbell, dumbbells, or kettlebells. Equipment, exercises, program, and goal are chosen independently.
Repeat strength efforts or sets with an emphasis on sustaining effort or repeating it many times, rather than only on a single maximal lift.
Train carrying, lifting, pulling, or holding heavy or unusual objects, or take part in Strongman events. Specify the objects and competition format separately.
Perform resistance exercises using strength-training machines. Specify the machine or muscle group as a workout detail.

entries.localizedLabel: Work out at an outdoor calisthenics park
entries.localizedDescription: Do strength or gymnastics exercises on outdoor bars and other available equipment. The park is context, not a separate exercise.
Perform exercises for trunk control and strength endurance. Specific exercises remain components of the session.
Practice the snatch and clean and jerk with a barbell or compete in these Olympic lifts. This differs from powerlifting strength lifts.
Perform strength and control exercises using bodyweight as resistance. Calisthenics may include handstands, pull-ups, and other skills.
Take part in an aquathlon combining running and swimming under the format of the relevant federation. The order and transitions follow the event rules.
Complete the running and cycling legs of a duathlon in the specified order. The standard version differs from a triathlon by having no swim leg.

entries.localizedLabel: Do a multisport or mixed workout
entries.localizedDescription: Combine several chosen movement or exercise types in one workout. The session determines the components and their order. This is not automatically a competition with a fixed set of stages.

Take part in an adventure race as a whole-event, multidiscipline competition. Rules, navigation, and the running, cycling, water, and transition stages depend on the organizer. Preserve the whole event and its activity legs as linked, potentially overlapping and non-additive views.
Alternate swimming and running along a route with multiple transitions between land and water. Equipment and stages connect the whole event; an individual run or swim may also be recorded as a leg.
Complete successive swim, cycling, and running or wheelchair legs in a triathlon workout or race. The event and its stages may be linked without double-counting time.
Play a cue sport on a table with a cue and balls. Pool, snooker, and other billiard games have different tables and rules, so specify the variant.
Approach and roll a ball down a lane to knock over pins. Scoring and repeated frames distinguish bowling from throwing games.
Throw darts at a marked circular target to score or subtract points under the chosen rules. The game mode can be specified separately.
Throw a disc from a tee toward a target basket on a course, aiming to complete holes in fewer throws. It shares golf’s course structure, but uses a disc and basket rather than a golf ball and hole.

entries.localizedLabel: Practice golf shots at a driving range
entries.localizedDescription: Practice club swings and ball flight at a driving range. This is range practice, not a round of golf.
Play a round by hitting a ball with clubs from the tee toward each hole, aiming to finish each in as few strokes as possible. Driving-range practice is separate.
Throw horseshoes toward a stake, aiming to ring it or land closer than an opponent. The task is throwing accuracy; the equipment does not make this an equestrian sport.

entries.localizedLabel: Practice equestrian sport, dressage, show jumping, or eventing
entries.localizedDescription: Practice equestrian sport by performing a dressage test, completing a show-jumping course, or taking part in eventing, which combines dressage, cross-country, and show jumping.
Strike balls with a mallet, guiding them through a sequence of hoops or wickets and toward the finishing peg. Turn order and rules depend on the game variant.
Play a chosen game in the boules family by throwing balls toward a target ball. Pétanque, bocce, and other boules games have their own equipment and rules; specify a local name when useful.
Aim and shoot a sport firearm or air gun at a paper or other target on a shooting range. Specify the discipline or weapon separately; this is not hunting.
Find checkpoints with a map or compass and choose their order or route according to the orienteering format. Running, walking, and competition are possible modes, not required by the definition.
Draw a bowstring and release an arrow at a target in a chosen archery discipline. Bow type, distance, target, and indoor or outdoor setting are parameters.

entries.localizedLabel: Do target shooting or a throwing event
entries.localizedDescription: Practice target shooting or throw a sports implement for distance or accuracy. Specify the exact discipline separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Compete in a horse race as a jockey
entries.localizedDescription: Race on horseback as a jockey, guiding a horse during a race. This is a mounted race, not spectating or barrel racing.

Cast a line, watch for a bite, and land a fish as a chosen competitive or recreational activity. The type of fishing and its rules are not specified by the label. This is not a target-shooting sport, even though casting takes accuracy.
Perform BMX trick sequences on ramps, street obstacles, dirt jumps, or a flatland area. The trick or line is the aim, not finishing speed as in BMX racing.
Start alongside other BMX racers and ride a short course with hills, rollers, jumps, and turns, competing to finish first. UCI treats this as racing, distinct from BMX freestyle tricks.

Ride repeated laps on a short mixed-surface course of grass, mud, gravel, or obstacles, sometimes dismounting to carry the bike. It differs from road cycling by surface and from mountain biking by course and race format.
Ride a mountain bike with electric pedal assist on dirt or mountain trails. MTB route and motor assistance are separate from racing or an ordinary e-bike trip.
Ride an electric bicycle, pedaling with motor assistance when available. Specify assist level and route separately. The vehicle alone does not say whether the trip is sport, transport, or leisure.
Ride a cycle propelled by hand or hand cranks. Hand propulsion describes the equipment; workout, recreation, transport, and para-cycling race are contexts that should not be inferred from the device.
Pedal a velomobile, a multiwheeled or streamlined cycle often ridden in a recumbent position. It is a pedal-powered vehicle, not a car or an ordinary bicycle.
Ride a bicycle on gravel roads and mixed-surface dirt roads or trails. “Gravel” describes a surface or cycling practice, not automatically a race event.

entries.localizedLabel: Ride an indoor trainer or virtual route
entries.localizedDescription: Pedal a bicycle mounted on a home or studio trainer or ergometer, and/or complete a virtual ride using a simulation or digital route. The trainer, indoor session, and virtual format can be combined but need not all apply.

entries.localizedLabel: Mountain bike: cross-country, trail, enduro, or downhill
entries.localizedDescription: Ride a mountain bike off-road. This is a user-selected umbrella type that can be refined to XC, trail, enduro, or downhill. XC includes pedaling over varied terrain; trail is riding on trails; enduro uses separately timed climbs or descents as its format specifies; downhill is a fast descent. Do not replace the full practice with only one subtype.
Ride a road bicycle mainly on paved roads. A workout, recreational ride, or race is the trip’s goal or format, not the discipline itself.
Ride a track bicycle on a banked velodrome for training or a track race. Fixed gearing and banked turns distinguish it from road cycling.
Ride a planned bicycle route as a leisure or tourism trip, often with stops or over several days. It does not require racing or sustained training intensity.

entries.localizedLabel: Mountaineer or make an alpine ascent
entries.localizedDescription: Follow a high-mountain route, using rock climbing, snow or ice travel, navigation, and rope techniques as needed. Mountaineering covers mountain-route activity more broadly than a single sport-climbing route.

Solve short climbing problems on natural rock or a boulder, or on an artificial bouldering wall, usually close to the ground without a rope and with a mat or spotter below. Outdoor and indoor bouldering are different settings of the same discipline; natural rock is included.
Climb a steep ice or mixed route with ice tools and crampons, usually with rope protection. This is not figure skating or speed skating.

entries.localizedLabel: Climb at an indoor climbing gym
entries.localizedDescription: Climb a set route on an artificial wall using holds. The format may be ropeless bouldering or roped climbing; specify the chosen route or type separately.
Climb a route with rope protection, using lead or top-rope. Protection mode and route may be sport climbing; bouldering is done close to the ground without a rope.

Perform a choreographed water routine with figures and coordinated movement solo, in a duet, or as a team. “Synchronized swimming” is an older or colloquial name for artistic swimming, not a separate discipline.
Catch a wave and ride it prone or on the knees on a short, buoyant bodyboard. This differs from stand-up surfing and from skimboarding near shore.
Paddle a canoe in a sport session or race. Specify either sprint over a marked distance or slalom through gates or a course, as these are different tasks.
Dive underwater with a self-contained breathing apparatus (tank and regulator) to explore or complete an underwater segment. This differs from surface snorkeling and breath-hold diving.

Practice diving or apnea without a self-contained tank. This may be static breath-holding at the surface, dynamic underwater swimming on a breath hold, or a depth dive; freediving is not limited to deep dives.

entries.localizedLabel: Row on water or an indoor rowing machine
entries.localizedDescription: Row a boat on the water or perform a rowing stroke cycle on an indoor ergometer. The first is water rowing; the second is training on a stationary machine.
Ride a board on water while holding and steering an airborne kite that pulls the rider. This differs from windsurfing, where a sail is attached to the board by a mast.
Paddle and steer a kayak or canoe in a chosen water or leisure format. Hull or paddle type, calm, sea, or white water, and racing are separate details.
Ride an ocean or artificial wave on a long surfboard. The longer board allows characteristic smooth turns and cross-steps; this is a type of wave surfing, not land-based longboarding.
Swim a long distance in an organized open-water race or workout. The event sets the exact distance and rules; this is a long-duration open-water format, not a separate stroke.

entries.localizedLabel: Sail or take part in a sailing regatta
entries.localizedDescription: Operate a sailboat during a training or recreational session. A regatta is an event or competition format, not a synonym for all sailing.
Swim in natural open water, such as a lake, sea, or river, without a pool lane. Temperature, current, route, and environmental safety distinguish the session from pool swimming.

entries.localizedLabel: Swim for rehabilitation or do aquatic fitness
entries.localizedDescription: Swim or exercise in water for rehabilitation, or do aquatic fitness. Specify the exercises and recovery goal separately if useful.
Swim through pool water using a chosen stroke or pace. Lanes, lengths, and workout plan are parameters; play or rehabilitation goals may be separate simultaneous meanings.

entries.localizedLabel: Spearfish or practice apnea as a physical activity
entries.localizedDescription: This combined category preserves two practices: (1) spearfishing—search for or take fish or another resource underwater using a chosen permitted method; breathing equipment depends on method and location; and (2) freediving or apnea—practice static breath-holding, dynamic underwater swimming on a breath hold, or diving without a self-contained tank, not necessarily to hunt. Do not reduce the whole label to only one of these two parts.

entries.localizedLabel: Go boating near shore for recreation
entries.localizedDescription: Travel in a small boat along the shore for leisure as a rower or passenger. Specify whether you operate the boat and how it moves—oar, motor, or sail—separately.
Jump or dive into water from a springboard or platform and perform aerial or rotational elements before entry. This is diving as a jumping discipline, not scuba diving.
Paddle as a team in an inflatable raft through rapids or fast-flowing water, steering the craft along a river route. Being a passenger on a calm-water trip is a different mode.
Paddle into a wave and then ride across its surface while standing or maneuvering on a surfboard. Board type, wave, and sport or leisure format are attributes.

Run along the shore and toss a flat board onto a thin layer of water or wet sand, then jump on and glide toward a breaking shore wave or perform flatland tricks. In wave skimboarding the rider actually rides the wave; starting from shore or shallow water distinguishes it from paddling out in deeper water for conventional surfing.

Swim or float near the surface wearing a mask and snorkel, breathing air above the water while observing underwater life. Brief dives may occur, but repeated breath-holds or depth practice are freediving.
Stand on a board and paddle with a long paddle to move across the water. SUP may be leisure paddling, surfing, racing, or fitness; the board is equipment.
Ride a wakeboard while holding a tow rope and being pulled by a boat or cable system. The pull is external, unlike self-propelled sailing or kitesurfing.
Glide across water on a board while steering a sail attached to a mast. Steering with a sail distinguishes windsurfing from kiteboarding, which uses a separate towing kite.
Glide across water on one or two water skis while holding a tow handle attached to a boat or cable. Do not confuse this with snow skiing.
Tour uphill in splitboard mode, with the board divided into skis, then reassemble it for an off-piste descent. The equipment and uphill access differ from an ordinary snowboard ride.

Travel on cross-country skis using classic technique where permitted: diagonal stride, double-pole or alternating poling, kick-double-poling, and other allowed classic variations. Unlike free or skate style, it does not use sideways ski push-offs as in skating.
Perform figures, steps, spins, and jumps on ice in a practice or artistic program on skates. This differs from recreational skating and speed skating.
Ski off a prepared or marked piste on natural snow. Freeride and backcountry overlap, but backcountry may imply remote terrain, traveling in independently, and separate avalanche preparation.
Descend a snowy slope on alpine skis, turning and controlling speed. A groomed run, lift, freeride, or race is context or a subtype.

entries.localizedLabel: Recreational ice skate at a rink
entries.localizedDescription: Glide on skates around a rink for leisure. If the session consists of figure-skating elements, speed racing, or hockey, choose that more specific type.

entries.localizedLabel: Sled or tube down a hill
entries.localizedDescription: Slide down a snowy or icy slope on a sled or an inflatable inner tube. Tubing and steerable sleds use different equipment, but both are recreational descents, not skiing.
Push a heavy stone over ice toward the target (“house”) and control its path or speed with sweeping under curling rules. This is not an ordinary throw or glide.

Play ice hockey on an ice rink or arena, skating and controlling a flat puck with a stick. The game includes skating, passing, and shooting. “On ice” and “with a puck” are clarifying names for the same ordinary form of hockey.
Glide on cross-country skis by pushing alternately sideways in a V-shaped skating stride, usually on a wide prepared track. This is not classic stride in a ski groove.

Ascend and descend a snowy mountain route on skis using uphill mode, such as skins, free heel, or a climbing binding. Ski mountaineering adds technical mountain travel or mountaineering sections; both scopes are kept in this combined label until a finer split is wanted.
Accelerate and complete a lap or distance on skates to achieve a time or placing. Racing line and strategy distinguish it from figure skating.
Walk over loose or deep snow in snowshoes that distribute weight and reduce sinking. A winter walk without snowshoes and skiing are different ways to travel.
Descend a snowy slope on a single snowboard, steering with its edges. A regular slope run does not imply park jumps or backcountry.
Travel on snow on skis or a snowboard using the pull of a steerable kite. This is not kitesurfing on water, though the pulling equipment is similar.
Walk a winter route on snow or ice. Boots, poles, or snowshoes may help, but the activity differs from skiing uphill or technical mountaineering.

entries.localizedLabel: Take a guided tour or walk
entries.localizedDescription: Walk or travel with a guide, following a route and listening to or viewing its points of interest. The place and mode of travel are context.
Take an unhurried walk along a city street or waterfront for leisure, observing the city and its life. If the goal is to get somewhere, it may be walking for transportation.

entries.localizedLabel: Take a coastal boat ride or boat tour
entries.localizedDescription: Be a passenger or guest on a leisure boat trip at sea or on another body of water to relax and enjoy the scenery. Operating a sailboat or rowing are separate activities.
Make a short leisure trip or excursion out of town or to a new place. The trip is the overall event; driving, walking a route, and sightseeing may be separate layers.
Spend time relaxing by the sea, river, or lake, without necessarily swimming or using a boat. Swimming or bathing may overlap in time but has its own tag.
Spend time relaxing and sharing food outdoors, usually seated at a chosen spot. Preparing food or traveling there may be separate concurrent activities.

entries.localizedLabel: Spend leisure time at the beach, sunbathe, or swim
entries.localizedDescription: Enjoy a beach outing by lying down or sunbathing, playing, or swimming without a set sport distance. Training swims and surfing are specified separately.
Spend time in an urban or nature park for relaxation and free-time activities. Visiting the place does not specify whether the person sits, walks, or exercises.

entries.localizedLabel: Visit a viewpoint or natural landmark
entries.localizedDescription: Arrive at a viewpoint or natural attraction and look at the view or feature. The climb, hike, or trip there is a related but separate stage.

entries.localizedLabel: Sit or rest outdoors, perhaps in a hammock
entries.localizedDescription: Spend time sitting or lying outdoors to rest or take in the surroundings. A hammock is one possible means of relaxing, not required or defining the whole activity.
Spend time near a campfire talking, watching the fire, or relaxing. Lighting or tending the fire is a separate practical task.
Walk for rest, experiences, or conversation, rather than to reach another required destination. Route, duration, and setting can be recorded separately.

entries.localizedLabel: Walk along a waterfront or through a park
entries.localizedDescription: Walk through a park or along a waterfront for a stroll or relaxation. Green space or water describes the setting, not a separate sport.
Walk a dog along a street or through a park. Pace and route can be flexible; feeding and caring for the pet are separate chores.

entries.localizedLabel: Take a road trip or scenic drive
entries.localizedDescription: Drive a chosen scenic route for the journey and views, often stopping along the way. A trip to a required destination may instead be ordinary transportation.

entries.localizedLabel: Take a safari or wildlife tour
entries.localizedDescription: Join an organized outing to observe wild animals on foot, by boat, or by vehicle. This is guided wildlife viewing, not independent species searching or hunting.
Observe a landscape for aesthetic enjoyment, without requiring a walk, guided tour, or photography.
Visit city attractions as a tourist, moving between places and choosing points of interest. This is broader than one guided walk, which may be a separate format.

Find and observe birds in their natural environment, noting species and behavior through visual, auditory, and other field signs. Visual searching and birding by ear are possible methods or subtypes, not the only meaning of birding.
Walk with a focus on plants, plant communities, and the natural environment, observing or identifying species. An ordinary walk may happen at the same time.
Take purposeful photographs while also walking. Photography and walking may both be retained as meanings of one event that does not overlap itself in time.
Photograph wild animals and/or read signs or tracks of their presence, without taking the animal. Wildlife photography and tracking are distinct but can be combined observation methods.
Search for a hidden physical container or object using GPS coordinates or a clue, then log the find under geocaching rules. The route to the location is part of the game, but driving is not required.
Notice and explore wildlife in an urban setting, including birds, plants, insects, and ecosystems, often including human-shaped places. This is not just a city walk.

entries.localizedLabel: Do citizen science or a species survey
entries.localizedDescription: Take part in a project field survey under its protocol: find or observe organisms and submit a record usable for science. Later labeling or validation may be a separate online session.

entries.localizedLabel: Interpret tracks or study local natural history
entries.localizedDescription: Explore a local natural area by identifying tracks, geological or ecological signs, and their context. Reading a guidebook without observing the site is a different format.
Look for and gather mushrooms in a natural area. Gathering may include checking edibility, but the purpose and local rules are not specified by the label.
Collect, verify, and connect documents, records, and testimony about family history. Visiting an archive, reading a document, and transcribing it may be separate research steps.
Find a hidden box using written clues or a route, locate its stamp, and leave a mark in the logbook. Unlike geocaching, the search is usually not based on GPS coordinates.
Watch the sky during a meteor shower and note visible meteors. A planetarium or recorded video is not field observation.
Watch animals living freely in the wild, aiming not to interfere. An organized safari or observing animals at a zoo has a different context.
Search for, observe, and identify insects in nature, often by shape or behavior. Catching or collecting them is not implied.
Observe local weather conditions directly, including clouds, precipitation, wind, and changes. Scientific recording of measurements may be an additional activity.
